schools.summary: Ellicott ties the ten years' quiet to Abijah's victory and to v.6, and glosses the name Asa; Keil surveys the older record of the pious king who reigned forty-one years.
Clarke, with Calmet, dates the peace from Asa's fifth to his fifteenth year; Wesley qualifies it as no open war but private hostilities with Baasha's subjects.
Henry makes the decade the reward of a godly beginning — Abijah's sword laid the ground for Asa's reforming peace, itself God's gift.

outliers.note: Qualifies the 'quiet': no open war, but private hostilities ran on between Asa's subjects and Baasha's.
With Calmet, reckons the ten years of peace from Asa's fifth year to his fifteenth, not from his accession.

schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'the good and the right,' distinguishes the foreign high places (removed) from the Jehovah high places (left standing), and reads the shattered Baal-pillars; Keil lists the chammanim sun-pillars cleared from every city.
Clarke: Asa attended to the law, and though not faultless was no idolater, suppressing idolatry universally.
Gill passes the verdict quickly, referring the reader forward to the reformation itself.
Gill traces the altars of the strange gods to the Zidonian, Ammonite, and Moabite shrines Solomon built for his foreign wives.
Henry: Asa destroyed the idolatrous altars as a provocation to God, hoping to reform the idolaters rather than ruin them.
Ellicott renders 'altars of the alien'; Keil adds the sun-pillars consecrated to Baal that Asa cleared from every city of Judah.

Ellicott finds the chronicler's own style and phrases — 'seek the LORD God of their fathers' (2 Chron 15:12), 'the law and the commandment' (Exod 24:12), the hammanim, and 'quiet before him'; Keil reads the command as the crown of the reform.
Henry: Asa obliged the people to seek the LORD and not the gods of the heathen, and to keep the neglected law.
Gill: the king by public edict commanded Judah to pray to the LORD alone and attend his worship.

themes: a reformation constructive as well as negative

schools.summary: Keil gathers the purge with the building that follows as one movement; Ellicott repeats that only the foreign high places were removed, the Jehovah high places remaining (2 Chron 15:17).
Gill distinguishes the wider reach of this cleansing and reads the images as sun-images.

themes: the purge through all the cities

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the fortifying in line with Rehoboam's and traces 'had given him rest' to David's rest (2 Sam 7:1); Keil grounds the building in the God-given peace.
Clarke reads the fenced cities as frontier defence; Wesley lifts the 'rest' into a meditation on the peace God alone gives.
Gill: Asa fortified against Israel and the nations, as Rehoboam had, perhaps rebuilding what Shishak threw down.
Ellicott notes the cities' names are unknown (Geba and Mizpah came later, after the Baasha war), reads 'the land yet before us' from Gen 13:9, and re-punctuates the verse.
Henry hears a ruler preparing in peace for trouble — 'when the sword is sheathed take up the trowel.'
Gill: the king addressed the nobles and principal men of the kingdom.

outliers.note: Would drop 'while' and re-punctuate: 'The land is still before us, for we have sought the LORD' — the building a fruit of the seeking.

schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil distinguish Judah's heavy shield-and-lance from Benjamin's light shield-and-bow, reckon 580,000 as the whole levy (no standing army), judge Benjamin's figure an overestimate, and hear the reckoning as a foil to Asa's trust in the LORD.
Clarke details the arms — targets with a central dagger, javelins, and the Benjamite archers' shield and sword for close fight.
Gill: Judah's large shields and spears for close quarters, Benjamin's shields and bows.

themes: trust in God, not the army

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies Zerah with Osorchon II and reads the invasion as Egypt's bid to re-impose its yoke, taking 'thousand thousand' as indefinite 'myriads'; Keil reports the usual Osorchon I and Brugsch's Ethiopian objection, and locates Mareshah.
Clarke places Ethiopia south of Egypt by Libya and doubts the forage for so vast a host; Wesley reads 'Ethiopian' as the nearer Arabian Cush.
Gill weighs African Ethiopians against Arabian Cushites, inclining to the Africans (with the Libyans), and reports Josephus' million.

sides.position: Ethiopians of Africa, masters of Egypt and Libya
an Egyptian army under a successor of Shishak
the Arabian Cushites, dwelling nearer to Judah
Osorchon I, on the usual identification
an Ethiopian, not an Egyptian, prince marching through Egypt
holders: Brugsch (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

debates.question: Is the 'thousand thousand' a literal number?

sides.position: a literal host of a million (with Josephus)
an indefinite hyperbole, 'myriads,' out of proportion to the 300 chariots

outliers.note: Doubts the logistics — a host from any great distance could never have found forage.

schools.summary: Keil locates the valley of Zephathah near Mareshah (not Tel es Safieh); Ellicott leaves it unidentified, noting the LXX's 'north of Mareshah'; both frame the king's turn from marshalling to prayer.
Gill marks the courage of Asa's going out against so vast an army.

debates.question: Where was the valley of Zephathah?

sides.position: near Mareshah, to the west or north-west (not Tel es Safieh)
unidentified; the LXX's 'ravine north of Mareshah' (a one-letter change) may be right

holders: Robinson (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

schools.summary: Keil (with Bertheau) renders 'none is with thee to help between a mighty one and a weak'; Ellicott presses a like sense, records Kamphausen's emendation, and notes 'multitude' (hamon) as Jeroboam's word.
Henry unfolds the prayer's four movements — God's sovereignty, the covenant bond, dependence, and God's own honour bound up in the cause.
Wesley: if the enemy prevail against us he prevails against thee; Clarke keeps the received sense and adds the Targum's 'in the name of thy Word.'
Gill: the king cried with vehemence, in distress, before the battle, for his army's encouragement.

debates.question: How is 'it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many or few' to be rendered?

sides.position: the received sense — God can save by many or by few alike
'none is with thee to help between a mighty one and a weak' — only God can help the weaker side
'there is none beside thee...'; or, by emendation, 'it is not for any to retain strength with (withstand) thee'

themes: let not man prevail against thee

schools.summary: Keil measures the overthrow — so many fell that 'to them was no revival' — and reckons Asa's army as God's host; Ellicott adds Thenius' corroboration from the dedicated spoils of 1 Kings 15:15.
Henry: God first defeated and disordered the enemy, and only then did Judah take the advantage he had given.
Gill: the LORD smote them with consternation and terror, a panic.
Wesley: smitten with terror and an unaccountable consternation.

Keil traces the flight to Gerar and the Philistine allies struck by the 'fear of Jahve,' reading 'no revival'; Ellicott prefers 'no survival,' a hyperbole of annihilation, and calls Asa's camp the camp of God.
Gill marks Gerar as a city of the Philistines.
Henry: the enemy fell before the LORD and before his host — an unseen army of angels or Israel owned as God's own.

debates.question: 'Could not recover themselves' — no revival, or no survival?

sides.position: so many fell that no rallying was possible (no revival)
utter annihilation — 'no survival,' a vivid hyperbole

schools.summary: Ellicott names the Philistine confederates and the 'divine panic,' and notes the late word bizzah for the booty against the classical shalal.
Henry: a fear God struck them with, so that they had no heart to withstand the conquerors.
Clarke: the cities held the army's forage, and to seize it Judah overthrew them.
Gill: Philistine auxiliaries and colonies of the invaders.
Ellicott reads the 'tents of cattle' as nomad Bedawin of the desert about Gerar; Keil records the sheep and camels carried home to Jerusalem.
Gill takes the 'tents of cattle' for the Scenite Arabs, tent-dwelling herdsmen.
Clarke takes them for Zerah's own cattle-camps and doubts the round million of the numerals.
Henry: the wealth of the sinner laid up for the just (Prov 13:22).

sides.position: encampments of nomad herdsmen (Scenite Arabs / Bedawin)
the cattle-camps of Zerah's own baggage-train, left in pasture

outliers.note: Owns that a host of a million is almost inconceivable and that there may be some mistake in the numerals, though the spoil was plainly vast.

themes: wealth of the sinner for the just
